pulls.title: Tighten the exclusion of protocol-version signals (OAuth 2.1 thread)
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Why

A comment on the OAuth 2.1 concurrent-version PR (`oauth-wg/oauth-v2-1` PR 268, comment 6671352444) argues for a per-request OAuth 2.1 signal. The argument is that a per-`client_id` switch can't be rolled out across the long tail of installed-app releases. OAuth 2.1 -17 now states in Section 1.8 that per-client configuration determines which rules apply, and it defines no version signal.

The draft already declined a version value, but on weak grounds:

- The Profiles appendix rejected it because "a version names a document". Choosing a behavioral name gets around that.
- The rule that actually excludes it lived only in Security Considerations (Downgrade). It wasn't in the invariants, which are the registry's admission criterion.
- The appendix offered the precedence override as "the general form" of the native-rollout requirement. That override points the wrong way for this case.
- The extension guidance on per-client rollout read, on its own, as endorsing a capability for this.

## Commits

1. **Normative.** Fold the enabled-check rule into CAP-1 so admission excludes it. As written, CAP-1 compares against "had the value never been defined". A value whose only effect is stricter validation passes that comparison when the client's configured rules are unchanged. The MUST NOT moves from Downgrade into CAP-1, and Downgrade now points to it. The deferred-response and txn-challenge cases still pass, because without the signal the server answers synchronously or refuses and skips no check.
2. Rest the version-signal exclusion on substance, not naming. OAuth 2.1's differences (Section 10) change what a client sends, what a server accepts and what a server issues. None introduces a response that a client conforming to RFC 6749 can't process: refresh token rotation is already required processing under RFC 6749, Section 6. Decomposing the version therefore leaves nothing to signal. What remains is choosing request-processing rules (wording corrected in commit 7). This commit cites OAuth 2.1 Section 1.8. It cites CAP-1 for the exclusion, so it depends on commit 1. If commit 1 is dropped, point that clause at Downgrade instead.
3. Correct which override a staged native rollout would need. The precedence rule lets a less-capable instance retract a default, but here the less-capable instances are un-updated releases that can't send anything. The approach that can work is the reverse: configured rules stay at 2.0 and updated releases opt up per request. Such a signal can't establish a client-wide security minimum while requests without it are still accepted (claim narrowed in commit 8).
4. Bound the per-client rollout guidance in Extension Guidance to behaviors that meet the invariants. This narrows the SHOULD NOT's condition to behaviors a capability could gate anyway, so no requirement changes in effect.
5. State the conformance exclusion in both directions. The old sentence was written for the RFC 9207 strict-parser case (a non-conformant client) and didn't cover a conformant client claiming conformance.
6. Name a protocol version (`oauth-2.1`) as a non-example in Naming Guidance.
7. Review: describe version selection as choosing request-processing rules. OAuth 2.1 also *relaxes* one check: Section 10.2 drops the token request's `redirect_uri` in favor of PKCE, so a version selector can make a server accept a request that OAuth 2.0 processing rejects. The stricter changes are what CAP-1 excludes. The lenient one is what CAP-3 excludes, because skipping a check when a signal is present relies on that signal. Extension Guidance now says "a change in request-processing rules" instead of "stricter enforcement".
8. Review: limit the claim to a client-wide minimum. Omitting the signal doesn't undo protection attached to credentials already issued under it. For example, under refresh token rotation the server keeps the token relationships (OAuth 2.1 Section 4.3.1). What a per-request signal can't do is establish a client-wide security minimum while requests without it are still accepted.

Each commit can be dropped on its own, except that 2 depends on 1, 7 builds on 2 and 4, and 8 builds on 3.

## Normative diff

Removed:
- Downgrade: "An extension MUST NOT use a capability to enable a security check that the server otherwise skips…" *Moved* into CAP-1 (commit 1), widened to name stricter validation of the client's own requests.
- Extension Guidance: "Where per-client or fractional rollout is a requirement, however, an extension SHOULD NOT…" *Condition narrowed* to behaviors that meet the invariants (commit 4).
- Out of scope: "a client that violates a MUST is not made safe…" A *mention* of a MUST, not a requirement (commit 5).

Added:
- CAP-1: "A capability MUST NOT enable a security check that the server would otherwise skip, including stricter validation of the client's own requests…"
- Extension Guidance: the narrowed SHOULD NOT above.

BCP 14 keywords: 83 → 82. The one fewer is the commit 5 mention.

## Left alone

- Appendix "Applying the Admission Criterion" still lists "behavior a specification makes mandatory to implement" among the rejections on gating grounds. Commit 2 now addresses OAuth 2.1 directly, so this PR doesn't touch it.

## Style deviations to review

- `OAUTH21: I-D.ietf-oauth-v2-1` is the draft's first bibxml alias. The other I-Ds use `target:` and `title:` and render as "n.d.". The URL form made idnits read `draft-ietf-oauth-v2-1` as revision 1 of `draft-ietf-oauth-v2`, which produced spurious OUTDATED_DRAFT, REFERENCE_NOT_USED and POSSIBLE_DOWNREF findings.
- `{{Section 10 of OAUTH21}}` is used instead of the draft's usual `{{REF}}, Section N` form, for the same idnits reason.

## Checks

- kramdown-rfc and xml2rfc build: ok (30 pages, up from 28)
- Commits 7 and 8 change no BCP 14 sentence
- idnits: same as main (3 appendix indentation findings and the stale DTR reference)
- Citations: none unresolved or uncited; no lines over 80 columns

pulls.title: Introduction: staged change to shared client metadata as a use
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Why

In the CIMD discussion of per-`iss` documents, the argument is that one Client ID Metadata Document can't stage a change one authorization server at a time, and rollback is global too. Per-request capabilities address this for optional behavior. The document lists what every instance handles, and each request names what its own instance handles, so instances opt in per AS.

The draft already has that mechanism: the metadata declaration rule and request-level precedence. The Introduction motivated it only through the two motivating extensions and the missing registration handshake. This PR adds staged change to shared metadata as a use.

## Commits

1. **Open-world section.** A new paragraph says a change to a published document reaches every instance and every AS at once, and rollback waits out AS caches. It uses `dpop_bound_access_tokens` to show the reach of any metadata field. RFC 9449, Section 5.2: "If the value is true, the authorization server MUST reject token requests from the client that do not contain the DPoP header." It then separates the two kinds of field. A field that *requires* a behavior can't be a capability (CAP-1). A field that only *declares support* for optional behavior can be, and capabilities split that declaration between the document and each request.
2. **Out of scope.** "Rollout cohort membership" now reads "rollout cohorts that a server assigns", so it doesn't seem to exclude a client staging its own adoption.
3. **Abstract.** One added sentence says a request-level signal lets a client roll out a capability one instance, release, or AS at a time, without changing metadata every instance shares.
4. **Extension Guidance (scope clarification of an existing SHOULD).** "Rather than define a dedicated parameter or field" becomes "rather than define a dedicated request parameter, HTTP field, or client metadata field". A future metadata field for optional client processing should therefore be a capability value.

## For review

- **Last sentence of the new paragraph.** "Every authorization server still sees the same document for a `client_id`" ties the intro to the per-`iss` CIMD debate. Drop it if the draft should stay out of that debate.
- **Precedence in the intro and in the Profiles appendix.** The intro cites `{{precedence}}` as what lets a request name its instance's set. The Profiles appendix says the precedence override doesn't provide a staged *native* rollout. Both hold: the appendix is about a default that un-updated instances would have to retract, and the intro is about updated instances opting in. The appendix's "what can work is the reverse" is the same model the intro describes.

## Normative diff

The only BCP 14 sentence changed is commit 4's SHOULD, which now names client metadata fields. Keyword count is unchanged (82).

## Checks

- kramdown-rfc and xml2rfc build: ok (29 pages)
- idnits: same as main
- Citations: none unresolved or uncited; no lines over 80 columns

pulls.title: Fix staged-rollout explanation: caches, retraction, cohorts, example
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Why

A review of the merged intro changes (PR #2, and 04c15f0) found five explanatory defects in the staged-rollout text. The normative rules are unchanged.

## Commits

1. **Make the staged-rollout paragraph accurate about caches and retraction** (findings 1, 2 and 4, all in one paragraph).
   - *Propagation:* "Reaches everywhere at once" contradicted the paragraph's own caching clause. "Every authorization server still sees the same document" overstated consistency: CIMD -03, Section 6.2 lets each server cache with locally chosen bounds and rate-limit fetches. The text now describes a shared change whose propagation the publisher can't target. The client still *publishes* one document for every server.
   - *Retraction:* Opting in or stopping by request only works while the value stays out of the document's default. Because a request set replaces the default, an opting-in request lists the instance's complete set. Once the default declares a value, withdrawing it takes a set without it, or `none`.
   - *Example:* The paragraph now leads with a deferred token response staged at one authorization server. DPoP stays as the boundary example: a field that requires a behavior isn't a capability, and staging changes to it remains a client metadata problem.
2. **Exclude cohort values whoever assigns them** (finding 3). a4e8ca4 narrowed the exclusion to cohorts "that a server assigns". A client-assigned cohort doesn't describe what a client can process either. This restores the exclusion with that reason, and says a client may use its own cohorts to decide which values to signal, while the cohort itself is never signaled.
3. **Limit the appendix's native-rollout sentence to version enforcement** (finding 5). Once 04c15f0 removed its context, the sentence read as contradicting the intro. It now says "a rollout of protocol-version enforcement".

## Checks

- No BCP 14 sentence changed (82 keywords)
- Build ok (29 pages); idnits same as main; citations resolve; no lines over 80 columns

pulls.title: Review round 3: interop fixes, wording fixes, and a Prefer rationale
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Why

Three cold reviewers read the draft: a WG reviewer, an implementer and a post-churn consistency reader. This PR applies the interop fixes and wording fixes from that round, and drafts an answer to the WG reviewer's main objection ("why not `Prefer`?"). Items that need the author's decision are listed at the end and are **not** in this PR.

## Interop fixes

1. **Request Object follows RFC 9101 §6.3.** The old text, "takes precedence over a duplicate value outside it", let an implementer use an outside value when the Request Object had none. RFC 9101 §6.3 says the server "MUST only use the parameters in the Request Object, even if the same parameter is provided in the query parameter." Outside values are now not used, and step 2 applies when the Request Object has no value. The value is a JSON string, and any other type is invalid.
2. **An invalid or over-limit parameter is present, with an empty set.** Precedence step 1 now says so. The field section claimed "absent, matching" the parameter treatment, which isn't true at an AS, where absent means the default applies.
3. **`none` in a metadata or discovery array makes it invalid.** Previously `none` matched the ABNF, so `["none","x"]` was undefined.
4. **Pointer to RFC 6749 §3.1/3.2 against repeating the parameter.** This guards against SDKs that encode arrays as repeated keys. No new requirement.
5. **"Only a hint" removed** from the deferred-response appendix. It contradicted Scope of a Signal.

## Wording fixes

6. Abstract: staged rollout comes from per-request sets, not from the replacement rule.
7. Profiles appendix: the OAuth 2.1 indicator is a "version selector", and it says outright that it would not be a capability.
8. Overview: the metadata default applies only to authorization server requests.
9. Terminology: `none` is registered only to reserve the token. Signal is defined as both the act and the values sent. "Signaled set" and "base OAuth" are replaced.
10. Syntax: the production satisfies both constraints and is narrower than either, not "the intersection". The section also says why it uses Tokens, since RFC 9651 §3.3.4 says "new fields are encouraged to use Strings".
11. Vary: the MUST is this draft's own requirement. RFC 9110 §12.5.5 only says SHOULD.
12. Seven smaller wording defects, listed in the commit message.
13. Example 3: retraction is shown by a registered client, not the shared CIMD `client_id`, and the example now says "instance".

## For review: "Why Not HTTP Prefer"

14. A new Design Rationale subsection. It concedes that RFC 7240 §4.1 describes `respond-async` as indicating "its capability and preference for handling asynchronous responses", and that `Prefer` could carry both motivating behaviors on direct HTTP requests. It then states what `Prefer` can't do:
    - cross the authorization-endpoint redirect;
    - be carried in a Request Object;
    - travel with a pushed request;
    - provide a client metadata default;
    - keep one vocabulary with an admission criterion.

    Drop or rewrite it if you'd make the argument differently.

## Normative diff

- Removed: "the authorization server MUST determine the request parameter value according to RFC 9101". It restated a dependency and is now a pointer to RFC 9101 §6.3.
- Reworded:
  - the invalid-field MUST;
  - the `none`-conflict MUST, now "the value as signaling the empty set";
  - the discovery invalidity MUST, which now also covers `none`;
  - the delivery MUST NOT, now aimed at `client_capabilities_supported` rather than "an advertisement".
- BCP 14 keywords: 82 → 81.

## Not in this PR (decisions needed)

- **Limits:** a minimum size every server must accept, and a single outcome for going over the limit.
- **Protected resource:** whether out-of-band knowledge applies when the field is present, and how to retract there.
- **The HTTP field at other AS endpoints:** introspection, revocation and device authorization.
- **Implementer pushback:**
  - the PAR SHOULD;
  - "SHOULD signal only advertised values" next to "MAY signal" others;
  - MUSTs on extension specs, which could become designated-expert criteria.
- **Replace-vs-union trade-off:** one sentence in Trade-offs.
- **A front-channel value sent next to `request_uri`:** RFC 9126's handling is not checked.
- **Missing examples:** a Request Object example, parsing test vectors, registration, CIMD and discovery examples, and a filled-in registry entry.

## Checks

- Build ok (31 pages); idnits same as main; citations resolve; no lines over 80 columns

pulls.title: Editorial pass: register, idiom, and tightening (no requirement changes)
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Why

An editorial polish and tightening pass. No requirement changes.

## Measurements first

The rendered body was compared with RFC 9449, 9126, 9101 and 9728 using `style_metrics.py`:

| | avg sentence | words per BCP 14 keyword | reason sentences |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RFCs | 16.6–21.8 | 63–114 | 8–10% |
| draft before | 17.7 | 65 | **14%** |
| draft after | 17.1 | 62 | **11%** |

Sentences were already as short as the RFCs', so the pass did not compress them. The outlier was explanation: reason, restatement and narrative sentences, and appendix text re-arguing rules the body now states.

Result: 8,183 → 7,665 words (−6.3%), 31 → 30 pages.

## Commits

1. **Citation form.** "Section N of [REF]", as in current OAuth RFCs. The two plural citations ("Sections 3.1 and 3.2 of [RFC6749]") are written as plain text before `{{RFC6749}}`. They render the same, and the citation checker reports the plural kramdown form as unresolved.
2. **Explicit anchors on every heading.** No rendered change.
3. **Heading renames (author's call, droppable alone).** Five clause or sentence headings become noun phrases, and anchors are unchanged:
   - "Why Open-World Deployment Makes This Urgent" → "Open-World Deployment"
   - "What This Specification Does Not Change" → "Scope"
   - "Signals Are Not Proof" → "Unverified Signals"
   - "Why Not HTTP Prefer" → "Comparison with HTTP Prefer"
   - "Why No Mandatory-to-Understand Semantics" → "Absence of Mandatory-to-Understand Semantics"
4. **Section editor A** (Introduction through Relationships): 18 edits.
5. **Section editor B** (Carriers through Extension Guidance): 12 of 13 edits. One was declined: cutting "Because the field does not necessarily identify the OAuth client", which is the only statement of why client metadata supplies no default for the field.
6. **Section editor C** (Considerations through Open Issues): 19 edits.
   - The Profiles appendix now cites the body's version exclusion (Naming Guidance, CAP-1) instead of re-arguing it: 545 → about 400 words.
   - The Prefer comparison is tightened, with every trade-off kept.
   - Examples open with "The following example shows".
   - Security, Privacy and IANA are unchanged.
7. **Seam repairs from the two post-pass readers.** This commit also holds four register fixes that were folded into it during an amend. There is no separate commit for them.
   - Restored:
     - that a `none` conflict doesn't fail the request;
     - the field's endpoint scope in Precedence;
     - which requests count as direct HTTP;
     - the "no OAuth 2.1 difference introduces an unprocessable response" premise;
     - the override premise behind "the less-capable instances".
   - Pointers and wording: "see {{no-require}}" replaces "see {{rationale}}". "Constrained instance" becomes the body's "less-capable instance", and "chiefly" becomes "such as". The ambiguous "which" in the PAR example is gone, and a duplicate citation is removed.
   - Register: "decide admission", "catches", "rather than aspirational", and "uses {{param}}".

The section editors worked from frozen edit rules. The rules held a keep list of every lowercase sentence added in today's review rounds, because the keyword record doesn't protect lowercase text. Each editor wrote a plan file that was applied only inside its owned sections, and I read every edit before applying it.

## No-normative-change proof (`noop_check.py`, main → 7b6b80d)

- keyword sequence identical: True (81 → 81)
- census identical: MUST NOT 24, MUST 49, SHOULD NOT 4, SHOULD 16, MAY 13, OPTIONAL 3
- fenced blocks 6 → 6, changed 0
- anchors lost: none (added: the 18 explicit anchors from commit 2)
- `condition_record.py leads`: 0 keyword sentences newly open a paragraph
- list, definition and heading line count unchanged (128)
- build ok, idnits same as main, citations resolve, no lines over 80 columns, no em-dashes

## Review

- **Obligation verifier on be5dca9** (after commits 1–6): it checked all 80 recorded keyword occurrences, plus one that wasn't recorded. Result: SAME 74, RESTRUCTURED-OK 6 (only the previous sentence changed), CHANGED 0, MISSING 0. All 23 keep-list items are present. Its conclusion: "no requirement changed". The one gap it found, the `none` "not fatal" sentence, is restored in commit 7.
- **Consistency reader on be5dca9:** "ready". Every seam it named is fixed in commit 7.
- **Commit 7 itself** got a targeted check, not a second full read: `normative_diff.py` against be5dca9 shows no keyword sentence removed or added; I read its word diff; and the noop proof above was rerun.

## Author's calls surfaced, not made

- **Heading renames:** commit 3; drop it to keep the originals. "Unverified Signals" is the one that most changes the original voice.
- **Security Considerations** has no opening pointer to Section 10 of RFC 6749 or to RFC 9700, which published OAuth RFCs usually include. Adding one adds a reference.
- **Unregistered-token collisions:** the risk that two parties give one unregistered value different meanings appears in Naming Guidance only. Security Considerations never mentions it.
- **Endpoint recording:** the rule that a registration records its endpoints still appears three times (the request parameter section, an Extension Guidance bullet, and the IANA Endpoints field).
- **Trade-offs:** the paragraph "The current extension count is small …" is narrative and was left alone.
- **80-column lines:** a few lines are exactly 80 columns and predate this pass (the Introduction blockquote and two IANA designated-expert lines). They weren't rewrapped.

pulls.title: Examples, PAR request_uri rule, and the replace-versus-union trade-off
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Why

This PR closes the three remaining items from the cold-review round: the replace-versus-union trade-off, the handling of a value sent next to a pushed `request_uri`, and the examples the implementer review asked for. The parsing test vectors are kept in the repository, not the draft (see the last commit).

## Commits

1. **Trade-offs: replace versus union.** A request set replaces the metadata default. So a client that adds one value repeats every default it still wants, and in exchange a less-capable instance can retract a default without a per-value removal syntax.
2. **Pushed `request_uri`** (a clarification that follows from the dependencies). A `client_capabilities` value sent alongside a `request_uri` from a pushed request is not used. The chain of dependencies:
   - RFC 9126 §4: the client uses the `request_uri` "to build an authorization request as defined in [RFC9101]".
   - RFC 9101 §5.2: `request_uri` "is used identically to the 'request' parameter".
   - RFC 9101 §6.3: the server "MUST only use the parameters in the Request Object".
3. **Examples:**
   - Request Object claims, showing the value as a JSON string, not an array;
   - a registration request declaring a default set;
   - authorization server and protected resource metadata excerpts.
4. **Illustrative registry entry** for the deferred-response behavior, marked "not a registration request". Its absent-signal behavior is the one already stated in Applying the Admission Criterion.
5. A rewrap of one over-long line in the Examples introduction.
6. **Verifier fixes.** The PAR and Request Object examples now say that a value carried there applies only to that authorization request. The registration example is aligned with the retraction example that follows it, the change-controller wording follows the template, and Trade-offs says "per-value".
7. **Public client in the registration example.** The example had registered `private_key_jwt`, but the retraction example it leads into sends no client assertion. That token request would fail JWT client authentication (RFC 7523 §2.2). The client is now registered as public (`token_endpoint_auth_method: "none"`); the token request already uses PKCE.
8. **Test vectors in the repository.** The tables are kept in `test-vectors.md`, linked from the README, not in the draft:
   - They pin down behavior still on the open-decision list: over-limit handling, and retraction and out-of-band knowledge at a protected resource.
   - They would cost five pages.
   - They would reletter the later appendices.

   A cold verifier checked every row against the body rules before they moved.

## Verification

- **Cold verifier:** it confirmed the `request_uri` sentence against the RFC text above and every new cross-reference. It also found every test-vector row correct. Its findings are fixed in commit 6. A separate review found the authentication mismatch fixed in commit 7.
- **Keywords:** the ordered BCP 14 sequence is identical to main (81), and no keyword was added.
- **Examples:** the six existing fenced example blocks are byte-identical.
- **Build:** ok, 31 pages. idnits is the same as main, citations resolve, and no line is over 80 columns or artwork over 72. No appendix is relettered.

pulls.title: Resolve open decisions: protected-resource retraction, field scope, pushback items, Security Considerations
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Why

This PR resolves five open items from the cold-review round. It **changes requirements on purpose**, so the no-normative-change proof used in earlier PRs does not apply. Instead, every changed keyword sentence is classified below.

The changes went through two reviews before this PR. A cold consistency reader checked a first version and found high-severity ambiguities about over-limit fields and empty field values. An external review recommended keeping the metadata MUST NOT and stating what stripping a narrowing signal does. Both are folded in.

## Decisions, by item

### 1. Retraction and out-of-band knowledge at a protected resource (commits 1–2)

| Field input | Effective set |
|---|---|
| absent, empty List, empty field value, or invalid | empty, subject to out-of-band knowledge |
| valid, at least one member | the field; replaces out-of-band knowledge, even if no value is recognized |
| `none` alone, or `none` with other members in a valid field | empty; replaces out-of-band knowledge |
| an invalid field containing `none` (e.g. `none, "b"`) | treated as absent |
| over a size limit | treated as invalid, so absent |

- **Why `none`:** an empty List can't signal "empty". RFC 9651 §3.1 serializes it by omitting the field, and §4.2 parses an empty field value as an empty List. `none` is the only reliable retraction. The current text already made a lone `none` an accidental retraction while forbidding it; this makes it the rule.
- **Denial of Service:** "signaling the empty set" was ambiguous at the field. A signal over a limit is now "treated as invalid": empty set for the request parameter, absent for the field.
- **Other places updated:**
  - the registry entry for `none` (adds the HTTP field and protected resources);
  - the transaction-challenge entry in the Existing Drafts appendix, whose out-of-band provision is no longer "unchanged";
  - `test-vectors.md`, which gains a table with out-of-band knowledge.
- **Transaction challenge:** the Existing Drafts entry now describes membership of `txn-challenge` in the request's effective set, rather than raw list membership.
- **Commit 2 (Downgrade):** stripping a narrowing signal widens the set. Removing a request override restores the metadata default, and removing a retracting field restores out-of-band knowledge. Both cause a failed exchange, not weaker security. Injecting `none` is the safe direction. Commit 2 also corrects the older Invariants sentence claiming that removing values always leaves the client with no capabilities.

### 2. The HTTP field at other authorization server endpoints (commit 3)

The rule keeps its existing scope, now spelled out: a client MUST NOT use the field where the request parameter is defined (the authorization, pushed authorization request and token endpoints, and any endpoint where an extension defines the parameter), and the authorization server MUST ignore it there.

At other authorization server endpoints (introspection, revocation, device authorization), the field plays no part. Precedence already says this for every request to an authorization server. An extension that needs a capability at one of those endpoints defines the request parameter there, which the request parameter section already allows. This follows the draft's design: the field is for requests that carry no OAuth parameters, and those endpoints all carry them. At the registration endpoint, capabilities are declared in client metadata. Adds RFC 7009, 7662 and 8628 as informative references.

This went through two earlier versions:
- A ban on the field at every such endpoint, which was unnecessarily restrictive.
- Letting each value's registration choose a carrier there, which conflicted with Precedence.

### 3. Implementer pushback (commits 4–7)

- **PAR SHOULD:** now applies when the client holds authorization server metadata that includes `pushed_authorization_request_endpoint` (RFC 9126 §5). No fetch is required, and server policies that require PAR are unaffected.
- **Discovery:** the SHOULD binds a client that holds the server's list. A client without the list MAY signal without retrieving it first. The self-cancelling "MAY signal values absent from the list" is removed, and the Privacy Considerations SHOULD gets the same qualification.
- **Vary:** required on every response that can vary with the field, including responses to requests that omit it. Otherwise a cached response selected without the field could be served to a request that carries it. `Vary: *` remains an alternative.
- **Extension-spec MUSTs:** kept. A designated-expert checklist item references their sections.
- **Kept unchanged, per review:**
  - **Metadata "every client instance" MUST NOT:** a default authorizes behavior on every request without an override, and the existing override exception already covers controlled heterogeneity.
  - **CAP-1 to CAP-3:** stay normative.

### 4. Security Considerations opening (commit 8)

"For general OAuth security considerations, see Section 10 of RFC 6749 and RFC 9700." Adds RFC 9700 as an informative reference.

### 5. Unregistered-value collisions (commit 9)

A new Security Considerations subsection. Two implementations can recognize one value with different meanings. Ignoring unknown values doesn't help, and authenticating the signal doesn't settle the meaning. The result is a failed exchange or wasted work, not weaker security. It points to Naming Guidance. No new requirement.

## Normative diff (`normative_diff.py`, main → HEAD)

Every removed or added keyword sentence is intended:

| Before | After | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| `none` MUST NOT be sent in the field; a recipient MUST ignore a `none` member | a field of only `none` is valid and signals the empty set (lowercase rule) | changed (item 1) |
| `none` with other values → "the value" signals the empty set | in the request parameter or a valid field → the empty set | widened to the field (item 1) |
| over a limit → "signaling the empty set" | over a limit → "treated as invalid" | disambiguated (item 1) |
| client MUST NOT use the field where the parameter is defined | … where the parameter is defined, with those endpoints named | same scope, made explicit (item 2) |
| clients SHOULD use PAR | … when the client holds metadata advertising it | condition narrowed (item 3) |
| clients SHOULD signal only advertised values; MAY signal absent ones | a client holding the list SHOULD; one without it MAY signal without retrieving it | MAY removed, SHOULD rescoped (item 3) |
| privacy: SHOULD restrict to advertised values | … when holding the list | condition narrowed (item 3) |
| Vary MUST on responses that vary | … on every response that can vary, including to requests that omit it | widened (item 3) |

BCP 14 keyword sentences: 69 → 68.

## Checks

pulls.title: Security completeness: presence invariant, access-control framing, downgrade, DPoP, profile appendix
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Why

This PR applies the security findings from the fresh-eyes review (WG, security and implementer cold readers, plus external feedback), along with the author's decision to trim the profile-selection appendix. **It changes requirements on purpose**; each changed keyword sentence is classified below.

## Commits

1. **Cover the presence direction in the invariants (normative).** CAP-1 covered only *removing* a value. A value whose presence led a server to pick a weaker control passed CAP-1 to CAP-3; only Selecting Among Alternatives blocked it, and that section is neither an invariant nor on the expert checklist.
   - **CAP-1:** adding a value MUST NOT lower the required assurance or lead the server to accept weaker client authentication, sender constraining, or user authentication. Among paths that meet that assurance, a value can affect which one the server takes.
   - **CAP-3:** the enabled behavior has to be safe also when a party other than the client asserts the value.
   - **Abstract and Overview:** their safety claims now rest on these clauses.
   - **Expert checklist:** adds Selection.
2. **A capability signal is not an access control.** Any party able to send a request, including one with a stolen code or token, can assert a value, elicit the enabled behavior, and choose among the paths Selection permits. That includes a challenge it could relay to another user, so each such behavior and path has to be safe in that party's hands. No new requirement.
3. **Separate request integrity from downgrade prevention.** A signed Request Object or a pushed request protects the integrity of the override it carries. An attacker can still substitute an unprotected request unless the server enforces the mechanism (RFC 9101 §10.5):
   - `require_signed_request_object` for JAR;
   - `require_pushed_authorization_requests` (RFC 9126 §5), or equivalent policy, for PAR.

   PAR enforcement does not require JAR. The commit also states that corrupting a field equals stripping it, and puts a condition on "removal never costs a server security property".
4. **Forbid promoting a request-level set to durable metadata (normative, SHOULD NOT → MUST NOT).** Otherwise one injected value becomes a lasting default for every instance.
5. **Qualify two overstated claims:**
   - Unregistered Values now says "provided each implementation meets CAP-1 to CAP-3 on its own".
   - The illustrative registry entry responds synchronously only if it can complete every check without deferral, and otherwise returns an error.
6. **Narrow the DPoP nonce rejection and correct the audit.** AUDIT.md said RFC 9449 has "no normative client requirement" for nonces. Section 8.2 says the client "MUST use the new nonce value supplied for the next token request and for all subsequent token requests". The two gating framings still fail. A third passes: server policy requires a nonce, and the signal selects between the challenge and refusal. Whether that warrants a value is a separate question. This commit updates the draft's admission appendix, AUDIT.md (adding Framing C) and the README summary.
7. **Trim the profile-selection appendix (about 400 → about 200 words).** It keeps the three agreed points:
   - version selection is policy and out of scope;
   - changed response processing gets a new value;
   - a removable selector cannot set a client-wide minimum, though protections attached to issued credentials persist.

   It cuts the WG proposal history (and the now-uncited `OAUTH21-VERSIONS-LIST` reference), the rollout recipe, and the `redirect_uri` argument.

8. **Finish the DPoP correction in AUDIT.md** (review round 2). Commit 6 corrected the worked example but left the ABCA comparison stale:
   - its table called RFC 9449's client requirement non-normative and said a capability was "barred by CAP-2";
   - its conclusion said the DPoP nonce was "outside this mechanism's reach entirely".

   The table now separates the retry after a `use_dpop_nonce` error (no keyword) from the success path (the §8.2 MUST), in both the client-requirement and advance-knowledge rows. The conclusion splits the nonce three ways:
   - nonce enforcement fails CAP-1;
   - token-lifetime concessions fail CAP-2;
   - offering the recovery challenge is admissible as a selection, and whether it is worth a value is a separate question.

   The "What this changes" finding now says it is the reliance framing that CAP-2 removes. No draft change.

## Normative diff (`normative_diff.py`, main → HEAD)

| Before | After | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| (none) | CAP-1: "Adding a capability value MUST NOT lower the assurance a server requires, or lead it to accept weaker …" | added (commit 1) |
| CAP-3: properties hold "even when the client does not implement the capability" | … "and when a party other than the client asserts it" | widened (commit 1) |
| "A server SHOULD NOT promote …" | "A server MUST NOT promote …" | strengthened (commit 4) |

Keyword sentences go from 68 to 69. No other keyword sentence changed.

## Checks

- Build ok (33 pages), idnits same as main, citations resolve, no lines over 80 columns.
- A test merge of #8, #9 and #10 after the round-2 commits is clean: it builds (36 pages), idnits matches main, and citations resolve.
- I checked the quoted text of RFC 9101 §10.5, RFC 9126 §§5–6 and RFC 9449 §8.2 against the RFCs.

pulls.title: Interop: none and discovery, invalid metadata, repeated parameter, size floor, CORS
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Why

This PR applies the interoperability findings from the fresh-eyes review, the external feedback, and the author's decisions:
- Size floor of 4,096 encoded octets and 64 members; canonical `none` is always admitted.
- A corrupted HTTP field stays absent (unchanged here).
- An invalid metadata member is ignored, scoped to `client_capabilities`.

**It changes requirements on purpose**; the keyword changes are classified below. It is independent of #8 and touches different paragraphs, so it should merge cleanly in either order. The test vectors are in this PR because most of them depend on its rules.

## Commits

1. **Exempt `none` from the discovery filter (scopes a SHOULD).** A client holding the list SHOULD signal only listed values, and the list never contains `none`, so a literal SDK could never retract. `none` is exempt; if filtering leaves nothing and an override is needed, the client sends `none`. Also: "bound fingerprinting exposure" holds only for a client that holds the list, and a discovery value that isn't an array is invalid.
2. **Ignore an invalid `client_capabilities` member (normative).** CIMD -03 §6.1 treats a document "rejected on trust or validation grounds" as a terminal failure, so `["none"]` could lock a client out at a strict server. A recipient now MUST ignore the invalid field and MUST NOT reject an otherwise-valid document or registration solely because of it. Handling of invalid JSON, failed signatures, and other required validation is unchanged. A non-array value is invalid.
3. **Repeated request parameter (adds a MUST).** A repeated `client_capabilities` is malformed and MUST be rejected with `invalid_request` (RFC 6749 §§4.1.2.1, 5.2). That differs from an invalid value, which isn't rejected. This also fixes "Like any OAuth request parameter", which overlooked repeatable extension parameters such as RFC 8707's `resource`.
4. **Narrow the unrecognized-values rule (rewords a MUST NOT).** A server MUST NOT reject a request *solely* because a value is unrecognized. An extension may still refuse when the effective set leaves no usable path, and a server may still reject an oversized signal or a repeated parameter. The old wording contradicted Denial of Service and Selection.
5. **Minimum supported size; protect `none` (adds MUSTs).** Limits MUST admit any otherwise-valid signal of at most 4,096 octets and 64 members, counted before deduplication or removal of unknown values. A table says which octets count for each carrier.

   A capability- or deployment-specific limit MUST still admit a parameter or field whose entire value is `none`, but not larger inputs that only reduce to `none`. The numbers are an engineering choice, not an RFC requirement.
6. **Hosted resources.** A resource that an authorization server hosts and that a client reaches with an access token, such as OpenID Connect UserInfo, is a protected resource for the field rules. Adds OIDC Core as an informative reference.
7. **CORS note.** `OAuth-Client-Capabilities` isn't a CORS-safelisted request header (I checked the Fetch Standard's safelist), so browser clients trigger a preflight. The resource has to allow the header; commit 12 corrects how. No new requirement. Adds the Fetch Standard as an informative reference.
8. **Transaction-challenge wording.** The out-of-band rule now applies when the request carries "no valid field with at least one member", matching Precedence, since an empty List parses as valid but is treated as absent.

9. **Test vectors** (`test-vectors.md`). New vectors for the rules above and for gaps the reviews found:
   - **Request parameter:** raw form-encoded inputs, including a repeated parameter rejected with `invalid_request`, plus case sensitivity and the 64-member floor.
   - **Request Object:** a `null` value.
   - **HTTP field:** duplicates, multiple field lines, a trailing comma, `none;x=1`, and canonical `none` versus `none` repeated past the limit.
   - **Metadata:** a non-array value.
   - **Discovery:** a new table.

   The commit also fixes the unrecognized-value row and the intro. Only cases the draft determines are included.
10. **Request Object octets** (review round 2). The table said which octets count for form-encoded values, fields and JSON arrays, but not for the JSON string inside a Request Object. The two readings disagree at the floor: 1,000 `\u0061` escapes serialize to 6,002 octets but decode to 1,000 characters. The count is now the serialized string in the decoded JWT Claims Set, quotes and escapes included. Adds escaped-string vectors on both sides of the boundary.
11. **Oversized metadata may be rejected** (review round 2, narrows commit 2's MUST NOT). Commit 2 said a recipient MUST NOT reject a registration because the field is invalid. Denial of Service made an oversized signal invalid and let the server reject the request. Those rules conflict: an array of `"a"` 65 times is only 261 octets but exceeds a 64-member limit. The metadata MUST NOT now ends "except as permitted by Denial of Service", as the request-parameter rule already does. Denial of Service names the outcome for metadata (ignored) and the registration error, `invalid_client_metadata` (RFC 7591 §3.2.2). Adds 64- and 65-member registration vectors.
12. **CORS wording** (review round 2, amends commit 7). The resource has to allow the field in its preflight response, most simply by listing it in `Access-Control-Allow-Headers`. A `*` value also covers it when the request's credentials mode is not `include`, which I checked in the Fetch Standard (§3.3.4 and the CORS-preflight fetch). The text cites `{{FETCH}}` without a section number, since it is a Living Standard.

## Normative diff (`normative_diff.py`, main → HEAD)

| Before | After | Kind |
|---|---|---|
| A recipient MUST NOT derive any capabilities from an invalid metadata field; the containing protocol decides | MUST ignore it and MUST NOT reject an otherwise-valid document solely because of it, except as permitted by Denial of Service | changed (commit 2), exception added (commit 11) |
| over a limit: a server MAY reject the request | a server MAY reject the request or metadata document | widened to metadata (commit 11) |
| discovery: invalid if an element is not a string … | … or the value is not an array | widened (commit 1) |
| (none) | a repeated parameter MUST be rejected with `invalid_request` | added (commit 3) |
| "Presence of an unrecognized capability value MUST NOT cause a request to fail" | "A server MUST NOT reject a request solely because a capability value is unrecognized" | narrowed (commit 4) |
| (none) | limits MUST admit ≤4,096 octets and ≤64 members; recipients MAY accept more | added (commit 5) |
| (none) | specific limits MUST admit a signal whose entire value is `none` | added (commit 5) |

The discovery filter exemption (commit 1) is lowercase text that scopes the existing SHOULD. Keyword sentences go from 68 to 72.

## Checks

- Build ok (35 pages), idnits same as main, citations resolve, no lines over 80 columns or artwork over 72; the new tables render.
- Commits 10–12 change no keyword count (72 sentences); `normative_diff.py` shows only the two sentences in the table above.
- A test merge of #8, #9 and #10 after these commits is clean: it builds (36 pages), idnits matches main, and citations resolve.

pulls.title: Worked adoption example and the authorization-endpoint carrier's purpose
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Why

Feedback from the fresh-eyes review: the examples stopped at requests, and the draft never said why the motivating extensions, both on direct HTTP, need the authorization-endpoint carrier. This PR adds no requirement.

## Commits

1. **What the authorization-endpoint carrier is for.** The carrier asymmetry section now says the motivating extensions need only direct HTTP requests, at the token endpoint and protected resources. The request parameter's coverage of the authorization endpoint anticipates extensions that change the authorization response. The PAR and Request Object examples illustrate the carrier.
2. **A worked adoption, from discovery to retraction**, as a new subsection at the end of Examples, in this order:
   - discovery (`client_capabilities_supported`);
   - an explicit signal on the token request;
   - **the changed response**: the deferred response from DTR §5.4, using DTR's own example values (HTTP 400, `authorization_pending`, `deferral_code`, `expires_in`, `interval`);
   - **the absent-signal behavior**: never deferred, so the request completes synchronously or gets an error under the grant's rules (DTR §4.3), shown as an ordinary token response;
   - **a metadata default and its override**: a registered client declares the value, its requests receive the default, and an instance that can't process deferral overrides with `none`.

   It points back to the existing example figures rather than repeating them, and shows both explicit signaling and overriding a metadata default.

3. **The synchronous example states its assumption** (review round 2). The 200 response assumes the authorization server can complete every check without deferral. Omitting the value rules out deferral, not failure, and the retraction paragraph now names both outcomes: a token response or an error.
4. **`Pragma: no-cache` on the example token response** (review round 2). RFC 6749 §5.1 requires it, alongside `Cache-Control: no-store`, on a response containing tokens. The deferred 400 response keeps the headers of the DTR §5.4 example it reproduces (`Content-Type` and `Cache-Control: no-store`). It is the only other HTTP response in the draft that shows these headers.

I checked the DTR wire format against draft-gerber-oauth-deferred-token-response-00.

pulls.title: Simplify structure: one home per rule (no requirement change)
pulls.author: mcguinness
pulls.body:
## Why

From the fresh editorial read: many rules were stated in two to four places, and some sections sat ahead of what they depended on. This PR gives each rule one home. **It changes no requirement** except removing two MAY sentences that duplicated the registry's Status field. One commit per item, so any can be dropped alone. #12 stacks on this one.

## Commits

1. **Define "out-of-band knowledge"** in Section 2. It was used about ten times and never defined.
2. **The request parameter's validity rule moves to 7.1**, its own section, like the field's and the metadata rules. Section 4.1 already said the rule "is stated with each" carrier. Pointers follow.
3. **The Request Object and pushed `request_uri` rules move from Precedence to 7.1.** "Step 2 applies" becomes "the parameter is absent for the purposes of Precedence", which has the same outcome.
4. **Requirements on extensions are collected in Section 10.** Three keyword sentences move verbatim, each with the sentence that carries its condition:
   - the absent-signal fallback MUST (from Downgrade);
   - the cost-analysis MUST (from Denial of Service);
   - the fingerprint MUST and SHOULD (from Privacy).

   The sections they leave keep their threat analysis and point to Section 10. Two lowercase duplicates go, and two designated-expert bullets merge.
5. **Restatements deleted:**
   - Section 5's "Two consequences follow" paragraph;
   - Downgrade's restatement of CAP-1 (its sentence on where a barred check belongs stays);
   - Selection's last paragraph, now a one-line pointer to Section 10;
   - half of the Prefer bullet in Open Issues.
6. **The version exclusion is stated once,** in Appendix C.5. Naming Guidance keeps a one-line pointer, and Section 10's duplicate goes.
7. **Obsolete status is left to the registry.** Naming Guidance's two MAY sentences repeated the Status field verbatim in substance. *This is the only keyword change.*
8. **One statement that neither signaling nor advertising a value obliges a server,** in Server Behavior.
9. **The unregistered-value collision is argued once,** in Section 11.4. Naming Guidance keeps its two SHOULDs unchanged.
10. **"MUST NOT promote" moves verbatim** from Server Behavior to Scope of a Signal.
11. **Section 6 (Relationship to Existing Mechanisms) folds into Appendix C.1.** Each entry restated an invariant or another section, and no section cited it.
12. **Two section pointers fixed:** Unverified Signals now points to where the Request Object text went, and an Open Issues bullet pointed at the wrong section on main.
13. **Escaped-string test vectors restored.** On main, the vectors added in #9's review round lost their escape sequences: the `\u0062 \u0063` row reads `b c`. My tooling decoded the escapes while writing the file. The Discovery intro now says "should", matching the draft's SHOULD.

## No-normative-change proof

- `normative_diff.py` main → this branch: the only keyword sentence removed is the duplicate MAY pair (commit 7), and none is added. Every moved keyword sentence is byte-identical.
- `condition_record.py leads`: one hit, the DoS "treated as invalid" sentence, flagged only because its pointer changed (Section 4 → 7.1). It led its paragraph on main too.
- **Cold obligation verifier**, against a condition record of main covering all 83 keyword records: SAME 74, MOVED-OK 7, CHANGED 0, MISSING 2 (the intended MAY pair). It also found six problems in the first version of this branch, all fixed before pushing:
  - Folding the Appendix C.3 path-selection paragraph changed what its exception covered. It is now kept as it was.
  - The obsolete pointer lost the optionality. It now says the change controller *can* mark a value obsolete.
  - An expert bullet dropped its "criterion" check. Restored.
  - Downgrade's "belongs in policy or an authenticated negotiation mechanism" was the only statement of that. Kept.
  - A pointer went half-stale after the Request Object move. Fixed (commit 12).
  - Selection lost its pointer to Section 10. Restored as one line.

  It also flagged loose phrasings ("which each extension analyzes", "this production", "three constructs"), all fixed.

## Size

Body 6,859 → 6,560 words (−299, −4.4%). Whole document 9,369 → 9,156. Appendix C.1 grows by the folded Section 6 entries.
